t.6.55.1: Then, having heard Aṅgada's words, those huge-bodied ones turned back, all of them eager for battle, having resolved upon a firm and final purpose.
t.6.55.3: And the monkeys, who had set out and been filled with joy, resolved upon death and abandoning all care for their lives, waged an exceedingly tumultuous battle.
t.6.55.2: Their valor roused and their prowess restored, those monkeys were steadied and brought back to their positions by the words of Aṅgada.
t.6.55.4: Then the huge-bodied monkeys, swiftly raising up trees and very great mountain peaks, rushed at Kumbhakarṇa.
t.6.55.5: That mighty Kumbhakarṇa, of enormous body, enraged, raised his mace and, tormenting his foes, scattered them on every side.
t.6.55.6: Seven hundred and eight thousand monkeys lie scattered on the ground, crushed by Kumbhakarṇa.
t.6.55.7: Gathering them up in his arms, sixteen and eight, ten, twenty and thirty at a time, he runs about devouring them, eating them in violent fury, as Garuḍa devours serpents.
t.6.55.8: Hanumān, stationed in the sky, rained down mountain peaks and many trees of various kinds upon the head of Kumbhakarṇa.
t.6.55.9: But mighty Kumbhakarṇa split those mountain peaks with his spear, and he shattered the shower of trees.
t.6.55.10: Then, seizing a sharpened spear, he rushed upon that fierce army of the monkeys; then Hanumān, seizing a mountain peak, stood before him as he came charging on.
t.6.55.11: Enraged, he struck with great force Kumbhakarṇa, whose body was as terrible as the greatest of mountains. Overpowered by him, Kumbhakarṇa then reeled, his limbs wet with fat and drenched in blood.
t.6.55.14: Then, seeing him distressed, the hosts of Rākṣasas, overjoyed, suddenly roared aloud; but the monkeys, distressed and stricken with fear, fled from Kumbhakarṇa in the battle.
t.6.55.13: His chest between his mighty arms pierced by the spear, Hanumān, reeling and spewing blood from his mouth, let out a terrible roar in that great battle, like the thundering of clouds at the end of an age.
t.6.55.12: Brandishing his spear, which flashed like lightning and blazed like a mountain whose topmost peak is aflame, he struck Māruti on the chest, between the arms, as Guha once struck the Krauñca mountain with his fierce spear.
t.6.55.15: Nīla hurled a mountain peak at the wise Kumbhakarṇa; seeing it hurtling toward him, Kumbhakarṇa struck it with his fist.
t.6.55.16: Struck by the blow of his fist, that mountain peak shattered, and, with sparks and flames, it fell to the surface of the earth.
t.6.55.17: Ṛṣabha, Śarabha, Nīla, Gavākṣa and Gandhamādana, the five tigers among monkeys, rushed upon Kumbhakarṇa.
t.6.55.18: With rocks and trees, with palms, feet and fists, the mighty ones struck the huge-bodied Kumbhakarṇa from every side.
t.6.55.19: Feeling those blows as though they were mere touches, he was not troubled; and he clasped the mighty, swift Ṛṣabha in his two arms.
t.6.55.21: Then the foe of Indra, having struck Śarabha with his fist and Nīla with his knee in the battle, smote Gavākṣa with the palm of his hand.
t.6.55.20: Crushed by the two arms of Kumbhakarṇa, that bull among monkeys, the fearsome Ṛṣabha, fell down, blood pouring from his mouth.
t.6.55.22: Tormented by the blows dealt to them and drenched in blood, they swooned and fell upon the earth like kiṃśuka trees cut down.
t.6.55.23: When those great-souled monkey chiefs had fallen, thousands of monkeys rushed at Kumbhakarṇa.
t.6.55.24: But all those bulls among the monkeys, mountain-like and of great strength, leaping up and climbing upon him as if upon a mountain, bit him.
t.6.55.25: Those bulls among the monkeys struck him, the huge-bodied Kumbhakarṇa, with their nails and teeth, and likewise with their fists and knees.
t.6.55.26: Covered by those thousands of monkeys, that tiger among rākṣasas, huge as a mountain, shone like a mountain overgrown with the trees that spring from it.
t.6.55.27: Seizing all the monkeys with his two arms, that mighty one, enraged, devoured them, as Garuḍa devours serpents.
t.6.55.28: The monkeys, hurled by Kumbhakarṇa into his mouth, which resembled Pātāla, came out through his nostrils and through his ears.
t.6.55.29: Devouring the monkeys, that mountain-like one, exceedingly enraged, the foremost of rākṣasas in his fury crushed all the vānaras.
t.6.55.30: Making the earth slimy with flesh and blood, that rākṣasa ranged among the armies of the monkeys like the blazing fire of universal dissolution.
t.6.55.31: Like Śakra with the thunderbolt in his hand, like Antaka with the noose in his hand, the mighty Kumbhakarṇa shone there with a spear in his hand.
t.6.55.32: Just as fire burns up dry forests in the summer, so Kumbhakarṇa burned down the armies of the monkeys.
t.6.55.33: Then those monkeys, being slaughtered, their troops struck down and left without leaders, shaken with fear, cried out loudly in discordant voices.
t.6.55.34: The vānaras, being slain in great numbers by Kumbhakarṇa, distressed and dejected in heart, went to Rāghava for refuge.
t.6.55.35: Seeing that mighty Kumbhakarṇa rushing toward him, the heroic Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, then leapt up.
t.6.55.36: That great monkey, lifting up a mountain peak and whirling it around, rushed with great speed at the mighty Kumbhakarṇa.
t.6.55.37: Seeing that monkey rushing toward him, Kumbhakarṇa stood facing the lord of the monkeys, his whole body laid open and exposed.
t.6.55.38: Seeing Kumbhakarṇa standing there, his limbs smeared with the blood of monkeys, devouring the great monkeys, Sugrīva spoke these words.
t.6.55.39: Heroes have been struck down by you, and a most difficult deed has been accomplished; armies have been devoured, and supreme glory has been attained by you.
t.6.55.41: Having heard those words of the king of the monkeys, filled with courage and resolve, Kumbhakarṇa, the tiger among rākṣasas, spoke these words.
t.6.55.40: Leave that army of monkeys; what will you gain with these common folk? Withstand a single blow of this mountain from me, O Rākṣasa!
t.6.55.43: Having heard the words of Kumbhakarṇa, he whirled the mountain about and suddenly let it fly; with that mountain, like the thunderbolt and lightning, he struck Kumbhakarṇa on the chest.
t.6.55.42: You are indeed the grandson of Prajāpati, and likewise the son of Ṛkṣarajas; endowed with renowned valor, therefore you roar, O monkey.
t.6.55.44: That mountain peak was then suddenly shattered upon his broad chest; at this the monkeys were at once dismayed, while the hosts of rākṣasas roared with joy.
t.6.55.45: Struck by the mountain peak, he flew into a rage and, opening his mouth wide, roared in fury. Whirling his spear, which gleamed like lightning, he hurled it to slay the lord of the monkeys and bears.
t.6.55.46: Swiftly leaping up, the son of Anila seized in his arms that sharp spear, adorned with golden garlands and hurled by Kumbhakarṇa's arm, and broke it with great force.
t.6.55.47: Placing on his knee that great spear of black iron, forged from a thousand bhāras of metal, the delighted bull among monkeys broke it.
t.6.55.49: Struck by the mountain peak, that lord of the monkeys fell senseless to the ground in battle. Seeing him fallen senseless on the ground, the Yātudhānas roared with delight on the battlefield.
t.6.55.48: Then, seeing that spear broken, the great-souled lord of the Rākṣasas grew enraged. Tearing a peak from Malaya, the mountain of Laṅkā, he approached Sugrīva and struck him with it.
t.6.55.50: Approaching in battle Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, whose valor was wondrous and terrible, Kumbhakarṇa seized him firmly and carried him off, as an exceedingly fierce wind carries away a cloud.
t.6.55.51: Having uprooted that mountain, whose form resembled a great cloud, and advancing into battle, Kumbhakarṇa, whose form was like Meru, shone like Meru itself with its towering and terrible peak.
t.6.55.52: Then, having lifted him up, the hero went off, praised in battle by the lords of the rākṣasas, hearing the outcry of the dwellers in heaven, who were astonished at the seizure of the king of the monkeys.
t.6.55.54: Seeing the army of the monkeys scattered in flight here and there, and seeing also the monkey Sugrīva seized by Kumbhakarṇa,
t.6.55.53: Then, having seized him, the lord of monkeys who was like Indra, the foe of Indra, mighty as Indra, thought: “With him carried off, this whole army together with Rāghava would be carried off.”
t.6.55.55: The wise Hanūmān, son of the Wind-god, reflected: "Now that Sugrīva has been seized in this way, what should I do?"
t.6.55.56: Whatever is fitting for me to do, that I shall do in every way; becoming like a mountain, I shall destroy the rākṣasa.
t.6.55.57: When mighty Kumbhakarṇa, his body shattered by fists, has been slain by me in battle, and the king of the monkeys has been set free, let all the monkeys rejoice.
t.6.55.58: Or else this king will win his release by himself, even if he were seized by the thirty gods together with the asuras and serpents.
t.6.55.59: I think the lord of the monkeys, struck down in battle by Kumbhakarṇa with the blow of a mountain-peak, is not yet aware of himself.
t.6.55.60: In a moment this Sugrīva, having regained consciousness in the great battle, will do what is beneficial for himself and for the monkeys.
t.6.55.61: But if this great-souled Sugrīva were freed by me, he would feel bitter displeasure, and his fame would be lost forever.
t.6.55.63: Having reflected thus, Hanūmān, the son of Māruta, once again steadied the great army of the vānaras.
t.6.55.62: Therefore I shall wait a moment for the prowess of our king, and in the meantime I will rally the shattered monkey army.
t.6.55.64: Then Kumbhakarṇa entered Laṅkā, carrying that great, struggling monkey, while those standing on the palaces, streets, houses and gate-towers showered him with the choicest flowers.
t.6.55.65: Then that great-souled one, regaining consciousness with difficulty while held within the arms of that mighty one, gazed upon the royal highway of the city and pondered again and again.
t.6.55.66: Seized like this, what indeed can I possibly do now, at this moment? I shall act in such a way that what is desired and beneficial for the monkeys will be accomplished.
t.6.55.67: Then the king of the monkeys suddenly seized him with his fingertips and bit Kumbhakarṇa, the enemy of the lord of the immortals, tearing his ears with his nails and his nose with his teeth, and biting him on his flanks as well.
t.6.55.68: That Kumbhakarṇa, his ears and nose torn away, lacerated and mauled by him, overcome with rage and his limbs drenched with blood, swung Sugrīva around and crushed him upon the ground.
t.6.55.70: Bereft of ears and nose, the mighty Kumbhakarṇa, drenched in blood, shone like a mountain with streaming cascades.
t.6.55.69: Crushed upon the ground by the one of terrible strength and battered by those enemies of the gods, he sprang up and swiftly went into the sky, and once again rejoined Rāma.
t.6.55.71: Then the mighty-souled rākṣasa Kumbhakarṇa, sallying forth suddenly from the city, devoured in battle that fierce army of vānaras, like the blazing fire at the end of an age devouring all creatures.
t.6.55.72: Hungry and greedy for blood and flesh, Kumbhakarṇa entered that fierce army of monkeys and, in his delusion, devoured in battle rākṣasas, monkeys, piśācas and bears alike.
t.6.55.73: Enraged, he seized monkeys with one hand, one, two, three, and many at a time, together with rākṣasas, and hastily flung them into his mouth.
t.6.55.75: At that time Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, tormentor of enemy forces and conqueror of hostile cities, enraged, gave battle.
t.6.55.74: Then the mighty one, though struck with the peaks of great mountains and streaming fat and blood, devoured the monkeys. Then those monkeys, as they were being devoured, went to Rāma as their refuge.
t.6.55.76: The valiant Lakṣmaṇa drove seven arrows into the body of Kumbhakarṇa, then took up other arrows and loosed them as well.
t.6.55.77: And passing by Saumitri, the mighty Kumbhakarṇa rushed straight at Rāma, as though splitting the earth apart.
t.6.55.78: Then Rāma, son of Daśaratha, employing the fierce Raudra weapon, released sharpened arrows into the heart of Kumbhakarṇa.
t.6.55.79: As he, pierced by Rāma, rushed forward impetuously in his rage, flames mingled with burning coals poured forth from his mouth.
t.6.55.80: The arrows fletched with peacock feathers sank deep into his chest, and the mighty mace, slipping from his hand, fell to the earth.
t.6.55.81: When that mighty one found himself without weapons, he wrought a great slaughter with his two fists and his two feet.
t.6.55.82: His limbs deeply pierced by arrows and drenched with blood, he streamed forth blood as a mountain pours forth its cascading springs.
t.6.55.84: At that time the righteous-souled Lakṣmaṇa, intent upon the slaying of Kumbhakarṇa and pondering many means, spoke to Rāma.
t.6.55.83: Maddened by fierce rage and by blood, he runs wildly about in every direction, devouring monkeys, rākṣasas and bears.
t.6.55.85: O king, he does not distinguish the vānaras, nor does he recognize the rākṣasas; maddened by the smell of blood, he devours both his own and the enemy alike.
t.6.55.86: Let the bulls among the monkeys climb well upon him from every side, and let the troop-leaders, according to their rank, stand all around him.
t.6.55.88: Having heard those words of the wise prince, the monkeys, delighted, climbed up onto Kumbhakarṇa.
t.6.55.87: May this evil-minded rākṣasa, when in time he falls to the earth weighed down by his heavy bulk, not kill other monkeys.
t.6.55.89: But Kumbhakarṇa, enraged and climbed upon by the monkeys, shook them off with force, as a vicious elephant shakes off its keepers.
t.6.55.91: Taking up his bow, fierce like a serpent, firmly strung and adorned with gold, and having reassured the monkeys, Rāma, his excellent quiver of arrows bound on, sprang forward.
t.6.55.90: Seeing them shaken off, Rāma, enraged and thinking, “This is the rākṣasa,” sprang up swiftly and took up his excellent bow.
t.6.55.92: Then that mighty Rāma, exceedingly hard to conquer, set forth surrounded by those hosts of monkeys, with Lakṣmaṇa following him.
t.6.55.93: He beheld the great-souled Kumbhakarṇa, crowned and mighty, the subduer of foes, all his limbs drenched in blood.
t.6.55.95: Him who resembled the Vindhya and Mandara mountains, adorned with golden armlets, streaming blood from his mouth like a risen rain-cloud.
t.6.55.94: Him, charging at all of them like an enraged elephant of the quarters, furiously hunting down the monkeys, surrounded by rākṣasas.
t.6.55.97: Seeing that foremost of rākṣasas, blazing with the splendour of a flaming fire, the bull among men then drew his bow and made it twang.
t.6.55.96: Him, licking up blood with his tongue, drenched in blood himself, crushing the army of monkeys, like Kāla, Antaka and Yama.
t.6.55.98: Enraged by the twang of his bow, that bull among the Nairṛtas, unable to endure that sound, rushed at Rāghava.
t.6.55.99: Then Rāma spoke in battle to Kumbhakarṇa as he came charging on, like a cloud tossed up by the wind and resembling a mountain, his arms like the splendid coils of the king of serpents.
t.6.55.101: Realizing, "This is Rāma," he laughed with a hideous roar, as though making the hearts of all the forest-dwellers fall.
t.6.55.100: Come, lord of the Rākṣasas, do not despair; I stand here with my bow grasped. Know me to be Rāma, O enemy of Śakra; within a moment this one will be bereft of his senses.
t.6.55.102: Laughing a hideous, terrible laugh like the rumbling of thunderclouds, the greatly powerful Kumbhakarṇa spoke these words to Rāghava.
t.6.55.103: I am not to be taken for Virādha, nor for Kabandha, nor Khara, nor Vālī, nor Mārīca; it is I, Kumbhakarṇa, who have come.
t.6.55.104: Behold my terrible mace, huge and made wholly of black iron! With this, in former times, the gods and the Dānavas were conquered by me.
t.6.55.105: You should not hold me in contempt, thinking, "He is without ears and nose," for I feel not even the slightest pain from the loss of my ears and nose.
t.6.55.107: Having heard Kumbhakarṇa's words, Rāma loosed well-feathered arrows; struck by them, which flew with the force of the thunderbolt, the foe of the gods was neither shaken nor pained.
t.6.55.106: O tiger among the Ikṣvākus, quickly display your valor upon my limbs; then, once your manliness and prowess have been witnessed, I shall devour you.
t.6.55.108: Those arrows, like thunderbolts, by which the finest sāla trees had been cut down and Vālī, bull among the monkeys, had been slain, did not then cause pain to the body of Kumbhakarṇa.
t.6.55.109: Drinking in those arrows with his body as though they were streams of water, that enemy of the great Indra whirled his mace of fierce speed and struck down the onrushing force of Rāma's arrows.
t.6.55.110: Then the Rākṣasa, smeared with blood, the terrifier of the great armies of the gods, whirled that mace of fierce velocity and put the army of the monkeys to flight.
t.6.55.111: Then Rāma took up the excellent Vāyavya weapon and hurled it at the night-wanderer; with it he struck off his arm along with its mace, and he, his arm severed, roared tumultuously.
t.6.55.112: That arm of his, like a mountain peak, severed along with its mace by Rāghava's arrow, fell upon the army of the king of the monkeys and crushed that host of vānaras.
t.6.55.113: Then those monkeys who remained of the routed and slain, having withdrawn to the edge of the field, dejected and with trembling limbs, beheld the most dreadful clash between the lord of men and the lord of the Rākṣasas.
t.6.55.114: That Kumbhakarṇa, his arm severed by the missile, like a mighty lord of mountains whose peak has been cut off, uprooted a tree with his hand and then rushed in battle at the lord of men.
t.6.55.115: With an arrow adorned with Jāmbūnada gold and charged with the Aindra missile, Rāma struck off that upraised arm of his, which resembled the coils of a serpent, together with the sāla tree it held.
t.6.55.116: That severed arm of Kumbhakarṇa, resembling a mountain, fell to the ground; writhing about, it crushed trees, crags, rocks, and monkeys and rākṣasas alike.
t.6.55.117: Seeing him, his arms cut off, suddenly rushing upon him with a roar, Rāma took up two sharpened crescent-headed arrows and in battle cut off the feet of the rākṣasa.
t.6.55.118: With his arms cut off and his legs severed, he opened wide his mouth, which resembled the submarine fire Vaḍavāmukha, and, roaring, rushed suddenly at Rāma, as Rāhu rushes at the moon in the sky.
t.6.55.119: Rāma filled his mouth with sharp-pointed arrows whose feathered shafts were bound with gold; his mouth thus filled, he could not speak, but groaned with difficulty and fell into a swoon.
t.6.55.120: Then Rāma took up an arrow like the rays of the sun, like the staff of Brahmā, like Antaka and Kāla: the unfailing Aindra shaft, keen-edged and finely feathered, swift as the wind.
t.6.55.121: That arrow, its lovely feathered end wrought of diamond and gold, radiant as the blazing sun and fire, with a speed equal to great Indra's thunderbolt and lightning, Rāma hurled at the night-roamer.
t.6.55.122: That arrow, driven by the arm of Rāghava, illuminating the ten directions with its own radiance, blazing to behold like smokeless fire, sped forth with a force equal to the thunderbolt of Śakra.
t.6.55.123: Then he cut off that head of the lord of the Rākṣasas, which resembled the peak of a great mountain, with its fangs bared and its lovely earrings swinging, just as Puraṃdara once severed the head of Vṛtra.
t.6.55.125: And then that rākṣasa, of enormous body and shining like the Himavat, fell into the ocean; it crushed crocodiles, shoals of great fish and serpents, and likewise entered into the earth.
t.6.55.124: Struck by Rāma's arrow, that mountain-like head of the demon fell. It shattered the houses along the streets and the gate-towers, and it brought down that lofty rampart.
t.6.55.127: Then the divine seers, the great seers and the serpents, the gods and the spirits, the Suparṇas and Guhyakas, together with the hosts of Yakṣas and Gandharvas stationed in the sky, were filled with delight at Rāma's valour.
t.6.55.126: When that mighty Kumbhakarṇa, the enemy of brāhmaṇas and gods, was slain in battle, the earth shook along with all the mountains, and the gods, in their joy, raised a tumultuous roar.
t.6.55.128: When that enemy of terrible strength, so hard to assail, had been slain, the many vānaras were filled with great joy, and with faces like fully blossomed lotuses they honored Rāghava, who had won what he desired.
t.6.55.129: Having slain in battle Kumbhakarṇa, crusher of the armies of the gods, whose strength in great wars had never been overcome, the elder brother of Bharata rejoiced, just as the lord of the immortals rejoiced on slaying the great asura Vṛtra.
